name: NREMT · Radio Systems & What to Say

cards.back: Transmit OR receive, one at a time, on one frequency. Push to talk, release to listen. You can't be interrupted while keyed up.
Transmit and receive at the same time using two frequencies, like a phone call. Either side can interrupt.
Sends two or more signals at once on the same channel, such as voice plus ECG/telemetry data.
A computer assigns the next open frequency from a shared pool to each transmission, so many agencies share few channels.
Receives a weak signal (portable or mobile radio) and rebroadcasts it at higher power to extend range.
Fixed radio at dispatch or a hospital, high power with a tall antenna. Longest range of the three radio types.
Radio mounted in the ambulance. More power and range than a portable, less than a base station.
Handheld radio you carry on scene. Lowest power and range; may need a repeater to reach dispatch or the hospital.
Sending data such as an ECG tracing electronically to the hospital or medical control for interpretation.
Mobile data terminal or computer in the rig: shows dispatch info and status buttons, cuts down voice traffic.
The FCC (Federal Communications Commission). It licenses frequencies and bans profanity and false info on the air.
Real-time direction from a physician by radio or phone, such as an order for a medication not covered by standing orders.
Protocols, standing orders, training and QA set by the medical director. You act without calling first.

cards.front: Before you speak on the radio
cards.back: Listen first to make sure the channel is clear. Press the button, wait about 1 second, then speak.

cards.front: How to hold and use the mic
cards.back: About 2 to 3 inches from your mouth, speak across it at a normal volume, slowly and clearly.

cards.front: How long should one transmission be?
cards.back: Short. Keep each one under about 30 seconds; break long reports up and let the other side acknowledge.
Use plain English. NIMS recommends plain language, and codes vary between agencies. Avoid slang and jargon.
Say "affirmative" and "negative" (easier to hear than yes and no). Say "copy" or "received" to acknowledge.
Never say the patient's name or other identifiers. Scanners can hear you (HIPAA). Use age, sex and condition.

cards.front: What not to say on the radio
cards.back: No profanity, no diagnoses you can't confirm, no judgments about the patient, no "please" or "thank you" chatter.
Repeat a physician's order back word for word (drug, dose, route) before giving it. Confirms it was heard right.

cards.front: Order that seems wrong or unclear
cards.back: Ask the physician to repeat or clarify it. Never carry out an order you think is inappropriate; document it.
Call: en route, on scene, patient contact if required, leaving scene/transporting, at hospital, back in service.
Call them, then identify yourself: "Dispatch, Medic 12." Wait for "Medic 12, go ahead," then give your message.

cards.front: Order of the hospital call-in report
cards.back: 1 Unit ID and level  2 ETA  3 Age and sex  4 Chief complaint  5 HPI  6 Past history  7 Mental status  8 Vitals  9 Exam  10 Care given  11 Response

cards.front: Report step 1-2: Unit ID, level, ETA
cards.back: "Mercy General, Medic 12, BLS unit, priority 2, ETA 10 minutes."

cards.front: Report step 3-4: Age, sex, chief complaint
cards.back: "We are transporting a 64-year-old male complaining of chest pain."

cards.front: Report step 5: History of present illness
cards.back: "Onset 30 minutes ago at rest, pressure radiating to the left arm, rated 8 out of 10, with nausea."
"History of hypertension and high cholesterol. Takes lisinopril. No known allergies."

cards.front: Report step 7-8: Mental status and vitals
cards.back: "Alert and oriented times 4. BP 158 over 92, pulse 104 regular, respirations 20, SpO2 95 percent."
"Skin pale, cool, diaphoretic. Lungs clear bilaterally. No JVD or edema."

cards.front: Report step 10-11: Care given and response
cards.back: "Gave 324 mg aspirin, assisted with one nitro. Pain now 6 out of 10. Any further orders?"
Wait for the hospital to acknowledge. Echo any orders, then sign off: "Medic 12, copy, clear."

cards.front: Verbal report at the hospital (transfer of care)
cards.back: Face to face to the nurse or doctor who takes over: name, age, chief complaint, history, findings, care, response and changes en route.
It lets the ED prepare the right room, staff and team, such as a stroke or STEMI alert, before you arrive.
Highest level: 24/7 in-house surgeons and all specialists, plus research, teaching and prevention. Handles any injury.
24/7 surgeons and comprehensive trauma care, but without the research and teaching requirements of Level I.
Prompt assessment, resuscitation and emergency surgery; transfers patients who need more to Level I or II.
Usually rural: advanced trauma life support and stabilization before transfer to a higher-level center.
Basic ED stabilization and transfer in remote areas. Not every state uses Level V.
Verified to care for injured children, with pediatric surgeons and equipment. Many protocols send seriously injured kids here.
Specialized burn care units. Take critical burns, inhalation injury and burns to the face, hands, feet, groin or joints, per protocol.
Highest stroke level: thrombectomy, neurosurgery and neuro ICU 24/7. For large-vessel-occlusion strokes, per protocol.
Can remove a clot from a large brain artery (endovascular), but has fewer specialty resources than a comprehensive center.
Can diagnose stroke quickly and give clot-busting drugs (thrombolytics); transfers patients needing thrombectomy.
Smaller hospital that can assess, give thrombolytics and rapidly transfer. Common in rural areas.
Has a 24/7 cardiac cath lab to open blocked coronary arteries. Many systems send STEMI patients straight here.
Has labor and delivery plus a NICU (levels I to IV). Take high-risk pregnancies or delivering patients here, per protocol.
Has a hyperbaric oxygen chamber: for diving injuries (decompression sickness, air embolism) and severe CO poisoning.
Small rural hospital (25 beds or fewer) that stabilizes and transfers. May lack specialty services.
For psychiatric emergencies once the patient is medically cleared. Medical problems usually go to an ED first.
ED not attached to a hospital. Limited specialty care and no admission, so check your protocol before transporting there.
Not a hospital: a hotline (US 1-800-222-1222) giving toxicology advice for overdoses and poisonings.
Closest appropriate facility for the patient's condition, using protocol, patient choice, and diversion status.
A hospital temporarily asks EMS to go elsewhere because its ED or a service is full. Unstable patients may still go there, per protocol.
